:::{#def-svd}
#### Singular value decomposition and singular values

Let $\matr{A}$ be an $n \times p$ matrix with real entries
and $\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}) = r$.
A **singular value decomposition** (SVD) of $\matr{A}$
is a factorization $\matr{A} = \matr{U}\matr{D}\tp{\matr{V}}$
with $\matr{U}$, $\matr{D}$ and $\matr{V}$ as in @thm-svd.
The numbers $\singval_1 \ge \cdots \ge \singval_r > 0$ on the diagonal of $\matr{D}$
are the **singular values** of $\matr{A}$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-svd}
#### An SVD of a $3 \times 2$ matrix

Let

$$
\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\matr{U} = \begin{bmatrix}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\
0 & 1 & 0 \\
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\matr{D} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\matr{V} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

$\matr{V}$ is the orthogonal matrix $\matr{Q}$ from @exm-spectral.
$\matr{U}$ is orthogonal too.
Entry $(i, j)$ of $\tp{\matr{U}}\matr{U}$
is the dot product of columns $i$ and $j$ of $\matr{U}$,
and those columns are
$\vecf{u}_1 = (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, 0, \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})$,
$\vecf{u}_2 = (0, 1, 0)$ and
$\vecf{u}_3 = (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, 0, -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})$:

$$
\ba
\vecf{u}_1 \cdot \vecf{u}_1
&= \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + 0 \cd 0 + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
&& \text{(definition of the dot product)}
\\
&= \tfrac{1}{2} + 0 + \tfrac{1}{2}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= 1
&& \text{(add)}
\ea
$$

$$
\ba
\vecf{u}_2 \cdot \vecf{u}_2
&= 0 \cd 0 + 1 \cd 1 + 0 \cd 0
&& \text{(definition of the dot product)}
\\
&= 0 + 1 + 0
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= 1
&& \text{(add)}
\ea
$$

$$
\ba
\vecf{u}_3 \cdot \vecf{u}_3
&= \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + 0 \cd 0 + \paren{-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}} \cd \paren{-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}
&& \text{(definition of the dot product)}
\\
&= \tfrac{1}{2} + 0 + \tfrac{1}{2}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= 1
&& \text{(add)}
\ea
$$

$$
\ba
\vecf{u}_1 \cdot \vecf{u}_2
&= \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd 0 + 0 \cd 1 + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd 0
&& \text{(definition of the dot product)}
\\
&= 0 + 0 + 0
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= 0
&& \text{(add)}
\ea
$$

$$
\ba
\vecf{u}_1 \cdot \vecf{u}_3
&= \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + 0 \cd 0 + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd \paren{-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}
&& \text{(definition of the dot product)}
\\
&= \tfrac{1}{2} + 0 - \tfrac{1}{2}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= 0
&& \text{(add)}
\ea
$$

$$
\ba
\vecf{u}_2 \cdot \vecf{u}_3
&= 0 \cd \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + 1 \cd 0 + 0 \cd \paren{-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}
&& \text{(definition of the dot product)}
\\
&= 0 + 0 + 0
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= 0
&& \text{(add)}
\ea
$$

The dot product is symmetric,
so these six values fill in all nine entries,
and $\tp{\matr{U}}\matr{U} = \matr{I}_3$.

$\matr{V}$ is symmetric, so $\tp{\matr{V}} = \matr{V}$. Then

$$
\ba
\matr{D}\tp{\matr{V}}
&= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(move the scalar to the front)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{bmatrix}
2 \cd 1 + 0 \cd 1 & 2 \cd 1 + 0 \cd (-1) \\
0 \cd 1 + \sqrt{2} \cd 1 & 0 \cd 1 + \sqrt{2} \cd (-1) \\
0 \cd 1 + 0 \cd 1 & 0 \cd 1 + 0 \cd (-1)
\end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{bmatrix} 2 + 0 & 2 + 0 \\ 0 + \sqrt{2} & 0 - \sqrt{2} \\ 0 + 0 & 0 + 0 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ \sqrt{2} & -\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(add)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{2} & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(divide by } \sqrt{2} \text{)}
\ea
$$

and

$$
\ba
\matr{U}\matr{D}\tp{\matr{V}}
&= \begin{bmatrix}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\
0 & 1 & 0 \\
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{2} & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd \sqrt{2} + 0 \cd 1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd \sqrt{2} + 0 \cd (-1) + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd 0 \\
0 \cd \sqrt{2} + 1 \cd 1 + 0 \cd 0 & 0 \cd \sqrt{2} + 1 \cd (-1) + 0 \cd 0 \\
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd \sqrt{2} + 0 \cd 1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd \sqrt{2} + 0 \cd (-1) - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd 0
\end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix}
1 + 0 + 0 & 1 + 0 + 0 \\
0 + 1 + 0 & 0 - 1 + 0 \\
1 + 0 - 0 & 1 + 0 - 0
\end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(add)}
\ea
$$

which is $\matr{A}$.
$\matr{A}$ has rank $2$, because its two columns are linearly independent,
and its singular values are $\singval_1 = 2$ and $\singval_2 = \sqrt{2}$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-svd-not-unique}
#### An SVD is not unique

An SVD is not unique
[@banerjee2014linear, Chapter 12, Examples 12.2 and 12.3, p. 378].
For any $i \le r$,
multiplying column $i$ of both $\matr{U}$ and $\matr{V}$ by $-1$
gives another one.
The singular values do not depend on which SVD is chosen
[@banerjee2014linear, Chapter 12, pp. 371 and 378].

For example, in @exm-svd,
multiplying the first columns of $\matr{U}$ and $\matr{V}$ by $-1$ gives

$$
\matr{U}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\
0 & 1 & 0 \\
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\matr{V}_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Their columns are the columns of $\matr{U}$ and $\matr{V}$,
some multiplied by $-1$,
so they are still orthonormal.
With the same $\matr{D}$:

$$
\ba
\matr{D}\tp{\matr{V}_1}
&= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
\tp{\paren{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}}}
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(definition of the transpose)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} -1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(move the scalar to the front)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{bmatrix}
2 \cd (-1) + 0 \cd 1 & 2 \cd (-1) + 0 \cd (-1) \\
0 \cd (-1) + \sqrt{2} \cd 1 & 0 \cd (-1) + \sqrt{2} \cd (-1) \\
0 \cd (-1) + 0 \cd 1 & 0 \cd (-1) + 0 \cd (-1)
\end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{bmatrix} -2 + 0 & -2 + 0 \\ 0 + \sqrt{2} & 0 - \sqrt{2} \\ 0 + 0 & 0 + 0 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{bmatrix} -2 & -2 \\ \sqrt{2} & -\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(add)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} -\sqrt{2} & -\sqrt{2} \\ 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(divide by } \sqrt{2} \text{)}
\ea
$$

and

$$
\ba
\matr{U}_1\matr{D}\tp{\matr{V}_1}
&= \begin{bmatrix}
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\
0 & 1 & 0 \\
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} -\sqrt{2} & -\sqrt{2} \\ 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix}
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd \paren{-\sqrt{2}} + 0 \cd 1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd 0 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd \paren{-\sqrt{2}} + 0 \cd (-1) + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd 0 \\
0 \cd \paren{-\sqrt{2}} + 1 \cd 1 + 0 \cd 0 & 0 \cd \paren{-\sqrt{2}} + 1 \cd (-1) + 0 \cd 0 \\
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd \paren{-\sqrt{2}} + 0 \cd 1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd 0 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd \paren{-\sqrt{2}} + 0 \cd (-1) - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd 0
\end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix}
1 + 0 + 0 & 1 + 0 + 0 \\
0 + 1 + 0 & 0 - 1 + 0 \\
1 + 0 - 0 & 1 + 0 - 0
\end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(add)}
\ea
$$

which is $\matr{A}$ again.
Both SVDs have the singular values $\singval_1 = 2$ and $\singval_2 = \sqrt{2}$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-svd-zero-singular-values}
#### Counting zero singular values

Some texts, and R's `svd()`,
also count $\min(n, p) - r$ singular values equal to $0$,
so that every $n \times p$ matrix has $\min(n, p)$ singular values.

For example, $\matr{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$
has rank $r = 1$.
Taking

$$
\begin{aligned}
\matr{U} &= \matr{V} \\
&= \matr{I}_2
\end{aligned}
$$

and $\matr{D} = \matr{B}$
gives an SVD $\matr{B} = \matr{I}_2 \matr{B} \tp{\matr{I}_2}$,
so by @def-svd, $\matr{B}$ has one singular value, $\singval_1 = 3$.
R's `svd()` reports $\min(2, 2) = 2$ singular values for $\matr{B}$:
$3$ and $0$.

:::
